title: Dietary urolithin a improves hepatic antioxidant function and laying performance in aging hens via Nrf2 signaling pathway activation

sections.abstract:
The decline in productivity and increased immune stress associated with hepatic oxidative stress in aging laying hens limit the efficiency of egg production. Urolithin A (UA), a natural metabolite, has been shown to activate the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway in mammals; however, its effects and underlying mechanisms in laying hens remain unclear. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the dose–response effects of dietary UA on the health and production performance of laying hens, with an emphasis on its role in activating the Nrf2 pathway. Fifty (45-week-old) Roman Pink laying hens were randomly assigned to one of five dietary treatments: a basal diet supplemented with 0, 50, 200, 400, or 800 mg/kg UA for 6 weeks. The production performance, organ indices, serum and liver lipid profiles, antioxidant status, immune markers, liver histology, and Nrf2 pathway-related mRNA and protein expression were assessed. An in vitro model of primary chicken hepatocytes was also used to validate the direct effects of UA. Compared with the control group (0 mg/kg UA), 200 mg/kg UA supplementation showed significantly improved the laying rate and egg weight, reduced the feed-to-egg ratio, and lowered the serum total cholesterol and triglyceride levels ( P < 0.05). This optimal dose also enhanced the total antioxidant capacity and superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase activities in both the serum and liver, decreased the malondialdehyde levels, and increased the immunoglobulin (IgY and IgA) concentrations ( P < 0.05). UA at 400 and 800 mg/kg doses did not enhance egg laying ( P > 0.05), but significantly reduced liver and abdominal fat indices ( P < 0.05). All UA doses lowered hepatic TC content ( P < 0.05), but only the higher doses (400 and 800 mg/kg) significantly decreased liver VLDL-C levels ( P < 0.05). At the molecular level, 200 mg/kg UA significantly upregulated the mRNA and protein expression of Nrf2 and its key downstream targets in the liver ( P < 0.05). These effects were corroborated in vitro, where 5 μmol/L UA significantly promoted hepatocyte viability and upregulated Nrf2 and downstream mRNA expression ( P < 0.05). This study is the first to provide systematic evidence that supplementing with 200 mg/kg UA may enhance late-phase laying performance by boosting antioxidant capacity, regulating lipid metabolism, and improving immune function, likely through activation of the hepatic Nrf2 pathway, suggesting its potential as a natural feed additive for sustained peak production.

Keywords: Urolithin A, Aging hens, Laying performance, Hepatic health, Nrf2 pathway
sections.introduction:
Decreases in production performance and immunological function in late-laying hens are significant challenges that hinder the economic viability of the egg industry ( Dai et al., 2021 ; Miao et al., 2024 ). As hens age, the cumulative metabolic burden of sustained high production, particularly regarding lipid metabolism and hormone synthesis, intensifies hepatic oxidative stress, disturbs redox homeostasis, and hastens functional deterioration in the liver, the primary organ for nutrient metabolism and detoxification ( Gu et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2023 ). At the same time, immunosuppression that occurs with age increases the susceptibility to illness and endangers the health of the flock ( Song et al., 2021 ; Walters, 2024 ). Nutritional strategies have been utilized to alleviate these challenges ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Gao et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2024 ), but their effectiveness in late-laying hens is limited, indicating a need for precision nutritional strategies to restore their redox balance and sustain productivity.

The Nrf2 signaling pathway is the main molecular regulator of liver functions ( Gao, 2022 ). When cells are under oxidative stress, Nrf2, a major regulator of cellular antioxidant responses, initiates the transcription of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. These proteins include heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) ( Ma, 2013 ). In high-production laying hens, however, the liver constantly experiences high metabolic stress owing to the production of high amounts of very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) to generate yolk ( Gu et al., 2021 ; Brouklogiannis et al., 2025 ). Under such physiological conditions, the liver endures extended periods of high-load activity, heightening its vulnerability to functional depletion and resulting in abnormalities in redox homeostasis ( Shao et al., 2023 ). Targeted stimulation of the Nrf2 pathway is an important measure to slow down the deterioration of the liver in the latter stages and sustain egg production at its highest level ( Li et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2024 ).

Plant polyphenols are secondary metabolites that arise naturally and have chemical configurations that are both hydrophilic and hydrophobic. They are found in many fruits, vegetables, tea leaves, and cereals, and have important roles in controlling redox balance, immunological responses, and energy metabolism in animals ( Mountzouris and Brouklogiannis, 2024 ; Pandey et al., 2009 ). Urolithin A (UA) is a significant bioactive molecule resulting from the gut flora-mediated degradation of ellagitannin polyphenols, and it is present in foods such as pomegranates and raspberries. It is recognized for its high bioavailability and exceptional safety ( Iglesias-Aguirre et al., 2023 ). Mammalian models show that UA can activate the Nrf2 pathway to boost antioxidant defenses and accelerate lipid metabolism ( Kang et al., 2016 ; Han et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2024 ). Nonetheless, the effects of UA on poultry, particularly late-laying hens experiencing significant metabolic and oxidative stress, and the mechanisms underlying these effects are not yet understood.

Therefore, this study sought to comprehensively evaluate the dose effects of dietary UA on the production performance, liver health, immunological function, and antioxidant capacity in aging laying hens. We also sought to determine whether the protective benefits of UA are associated with the direct activation of the hepatic Nrf2 signaling pathway. This study provides a robust theoretical and experimental basis for the development of novel natural feed additives.
sections.methods:
Fifty Roman Pink laying hens, aged 45 weeks, were selected from an indoor flock of 425 hens. Following the initial weight recording (mean ± standard deviation = 1785 ± 77 g), the hens were randomly distributed into five treatment groups, each containing 10 birds, to serve as individual experimental units. The hens were housed in a three-tier wire mesh cage system (50 × 60 × 37 cm) equipped with nipple drinkers and open-trough feeders. After a 1-week acclimatization period, a formal 6-week trial was conducted. The environmental conditions within the facility were maintained through daily manual regulation of the side-wall shade curtains. This management practice maintained a stable temperature of 21–24 °C, a 12-hour light photoperiod, and sufficient ventilation to protect bird health. Animals had unrestricted access to food and water.

Laying hens were distributed into five dietary treatments based on comparable body weights. Each treatment group consisted of 10 replicates, with each replicate containing one bird. In this study, each hen was housed individually, thereby serving as an independent experimental unit. The birds randomly distributed to the cages. The control group (CON) received a basal diet, while the four treatment groups received the same basal diet supplemented with UA (purity ≥ 99 %, Chengdu Desite Biological Technologies Co. Ltd., CAS: 1143-70-0) at graded levels of 50, 200, 400, or 800 mg/kg feed. The high purity of UA was verified using high-performance liquid chromatography. At the end of the feeding trial, 10 birds per group were euthanized and samples were obtained. The formulation and nutritional composition of the basal diet are presented in Table 1 ( NRC, 1994 ).

Ingredients and nutrients in the experimental basal diet (as-fed basis, %).

Composition per kg of premix: VA, 10000 IU/kg; VD3, 3000 IU/kg; VE, 20 IU/kg; VK, 32 mg/kg; thiamine, 1 mg/kg; riboflavin, 8 mg/kg; calcium pantothenate, 40 mg/kg; niacin, 32.5 mg/kg; pyridoxine, 8 mg/kg; biotin, 2 mg/kg; folic acid, 1.5 mg/kg; VB12, 5 mg/kg; choline, 500 mg/kg; Mn, 70 mg/kg; I, 1 mg/kg; Fe, 80 mg/kg; Cu, 8 mg/kg; Zn, 80 mg/kg.

Calculated values according to data from the Chinese table of feed ingredients and nutritional values. Abbreviation: ME = metabolizable energy.

In this trial, fresh feed was supplied daily, and intake was recorded daily in grams per hen. Experimental diets were provided once daily at 07:00. The following morning, before fresh feed was allocated, any remaining feed was collected and weighed. Daily feed intake per replicate was determined by subtracting the remaining feed weight from the previous day's feed weight. The average daily feed intake per hen was calculated by dividing the total feed intake by one hen in each replicate. Eggs were collected and laying rates were recorded daily. Egg weight (g) was recorded daily using an electronic scale. The feed-egg-ratio was calculated by dividing the daily feed consumption by the average egg weight. Performance was calculated for both the 3- and 6-week experimental periods.

After the hens had fasted for 8 h straight, 5 mL of blood was drawn at the end of the experiment. These samples were centrifuged at 2,000 × g for 10 min at a 4 °C to extract the serum. Subsequently, the serum was divided into equal portions and stored at -80 °C in a freezer. The animals were then euthanized, and the liver and abdominal fat were excised and weighed. Liver tissue samples were systematically collected from the left lobe using a Vernier caliper to standardize the sampling area, with 10 samples collected per group. While four samples were placed in 4 % paraformaldehyde to evaluate their structural characteristics, while the remaining six samples were rapidly frozen at -80 °C for further biochemical testing, RNA separation, and qRT-PCR analysis. The organ index was computed by dividing the weight of the spleen or abdominal fat by the final body weight.

After being properly preserved, the liver samples were dehydrated in graded alcohol and then treated with xylene to make them transparent. Subsequently, the material was sliced into 5 µm-thick pieces and submerged in paraffin wax. Hematoxylin and eosin staining was then used to analyze the overall architecture of these tissue slices. Microscopic examination was carried out with an Olympus DP80 digital imaging system (Tokyo, Japan), and 10 fields per sample were randomly chosen for statistical evaluation.

As this study represents a pioneering dose-response evaluation of UA in poultry, a broad spectrum of biochemical parameters was assessed to ensure a holistic safety and efficacy profile. Beyond the primary endpoints of antioxidant function and lipid metabolism, key indicators of immune status (serum and hepatic immunoglobulins) and liver cell integrity (serum and hepatic enzymes) were measured to fully characterize the physiological impact of UA supplementation.

Homogenates of the liver tissue and serum were prepared according to the protocols supplied by the Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (China). We calculated the liver antioxidant parameters and measured the amount of protein in the supernatant using a commercial total protein assay kit. To evaluate various metabolic and inflammatory conditions, we ran biochemical tests on the liver and serum samples. To assess the level of oxidative stress and liver function, we used kits from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute to measure glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px), catalase (CAT), malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC), and total superoxide dismutase (T-SOD). For lipid profiles, levels of total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), very low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (VLDL-C), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were measured. Additionally, immunological markers such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), immunoglobulin A (IgA), and immunoglobulin Y (IgY) were analyzed using ELISA kits (Shanghai Youxuan Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Primary hepatocytes were aseptically isolated from Roman Pink laying hens (n = 4) using a standard protocol ( Qi et al., 2018 ; Cui et al., 2022 ). After quantification, the cells were resuspended in William’s E medium (Sigma, Shanghai) and plated in 6-well plates at a density of 2 × 10⁶ cells/well. Cultures were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5 % CO₂. Cell viability was assessed via CCK-8 assay (Melon Bio, Dalian) to determine the optimal concentration of UA. For 24 hours, the hepatocytes were subjected to a variety of UA concentrations (0, 1, 5, 50, 100, 200, 400, and 800 μmol/L). Each well was then filled with 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent, and the mixture was incubated for 2 h. A Varioskan LUX microplate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) was used to measure absorbance at 450 nm. A UA concentration of 5 μmol/L was chosen for further research into its effects on the Nrf2 signaling pathway based on the viability results.

To lyse liver tissue samples and primary hepatocytes, a protease inhibitor cocktail was added to RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). Following this disruption, the samples were kept at 4 °C and centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 15 min. After the supernatant was carefully collected, the protein contents were measured. Matching protein amounts were immobilized on PVDF membranes (Merck Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA) after SDS-PAGE fractionation. The membranes were exposed to 5 % non-fat milk for 1 h at room temperature to avoid non-specific binding. Subsequently, primary antibodies against GAPDH (1:10,000; Proteintech) and Nrf2 (1:3,000; Wuhan Sanying Biotechnology) were applied to the membranes overnight and stored in a refrigerator. After the primary antibody treatment, the membranes were subjected to an HRP-linked goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (1:6,000; Proteintech) for 1 h at room temperature. Protein expression was visualized using a ChemiDocTM XRS + imaging system (Bio-Rad, USA) and an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) detection kit (Tanon, Shanghai, China). Band intensity was quantitatively measured using ImageJ software (NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA).

To ensure specificity, the qPCR primers ( Table 2 ) were developed using NCBI PrimerBlast with stringent requirements (amplicon size, 80–200 bp; Tm, 58–62 °C; GC content, 40–60 %). Total RNA was extracted from the liver and primary hepatocytes using TRIzol reagent (Takara, Shiga, Japan) based on the manufacturer's instructions. RNA was quantified using a bio-photometer (NanoDrop2000; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), and its quality was evaluated using agarose gel electrophoresis. Reverse transcription was performed using 10 μL of reaction mixture, which contained 1000 ng of RNA, 5 mmol/L MgCl2, 1 μL of RT buffer, 1 mmol/L dNTP, 2.5 U of AMV, 0.7 nmol/L oligodeoxynucleotides d(T), and 10 U of ribonuclease inhibitor (TaKaRa, Dalian, China). Real-time PCR was performed using a Bio-Rad CFXConnect TM system (Bio-Rad, USA). Each real-time PCR result was used as a template in a 20 μL PCR reaction with 0.2 μmol/L of each primer and SYBR Green premix (Accurate Biology, Hunan, China). The PCR procedure included initial denaturation at 95 °C for 10 s, followed by 60 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 30 s. GAPDH used as the housekeeping gene. The relative mRNA expression levels were assessed using the comparative Ct method (2 −ΔΔCt ), which was consistent with the normalization methodology. The amplification's specificity was verified using melting-curve analysis.

Real-time fluorescent quantitative PCR primers.

Abbreviations: Nrf2 = Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2; HO-1 = Heme oxygenase-1; NQO1 = NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1; GPX4 = Glutathione peroxidase 4; SLC7A11 = Solute carrier family 7 member 11; GAPDH = Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase.

Group differences were evaluated using one-way ANOVA and Duncan's multiple range test with GraphPad Prism 8.0 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA). Data are presented as the means with their standard errors. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05. Spearman's correlation coefficients were applied for continuous data, whereas point-biserial correlations were used for binary data. The correlations were categorized as weak (|r| < 0.33), moderate (0.33 ≤ |r| < 0.66), or strong (|r| ≥ 0.66) using the LinkET package in R.
sections.results:
The laying performance of Roman Pink laying hens is shown in Fig. 1 A and B. Over both the 3- and 6-week intervals, hens fed diets supplemented with 50 and 200 mg/kg UA exhibited increased egg weights ( P < 0.05) and decreased feed-to-egg ratios compared with those fed the CON diet ( P < 0.05). Additionally, hens fed the diet supplemented with 200 mg/kg UA showed a higher laying rate than those fed the CON diet ( P < 0.05). However, there was no difference in the average daily feed intake among the five experimental groups ( P > 0.05).

Effect of dietary urolithin A (UA) supplementation on laying performance and liver and abdominal fat indices in Roman Pink laying hens (n = 10). (A–D) Laying performance at 3 weeks. (E–H) Laying performance at 6 weeks. (I–L) Liver and abdominal fat weights and indices. (M) Flow chart of the in vitro experimental studies. (N) Correlation (Spearman) between dietary UA addition and liver and abdominal fat indices and laying performance. Multiple comparisons were performed between each treatment group and the control using Duncan’s multiple range test (same applies below). Solid lines represent a significance level of P < 0.05, while dashed lines denote P > 0.05. The thickness of the lines corresponds to the magnitude of the correlation coefficients: thin lines indicate |r| < 0.33, medium lines indicate 0.33 ≤ |r| < 0.66, and thick lines indicate 0.66 ≤ |r| < 1. Blue lines illustrate negative correlations, whereas orange lines depict positive correlations (the same applies below).

The liver and abdominal fat weights and indices of Roman Pink laying hens are shown in Fig. 1 C. The liver weight and index were lower in hens fed diets supplemented with 200, 400, and 800 mg/kg UA than in those fed the CON diet ( P < 0.05). Furthermore, the abdominal fat weight and index were lower in hens fed diets supplemented with 400 and 800 mg/kg UA than in those fed the CON diet ( P < 0.05). In addition, the laying rate and egg weight were both negatively correlated with liver and abdominal fat ( P < 0.05), indicating a possible energy trade-off between laying performance and fat storage. Moreover, the level of UA supplementation was negatively correlated with both the liver and abdominal fat indices ( P < 0.05; Fig. 1 E).

The effects of dietary UA supplementation on lipid metabolism in the serum and liver of Roman Pink laying hens are shown in Fig. 2 A and B, respectively. Compared with the CON diet, the 200 mg/kg UA diet lowered the serum TC and TG levels in laying hens ( P < 0.05), the 50 mg/kg UA diet reduced the TC concentration ( P < 0.05), and the 400 and 800 mg/kg UA diets decreased the TG concentration ( P < 0.05). Laying hens fed the diet with 400 mg/kg UA exhibited increased serum HDL-C levels and decreased VLDL-C concentrations compared to those on the CON diet ( P < 0.05). Laying hens fed diets with 50, 200, 400, and 800 mg/kg UA showed reduced liver TC content compared to those on the CON diet ( P < 0.05). Hens fed diets supplemented with 400 and 800 mg/kg of UA showed significantly increased liver HDL-C levels ( P < 0.05), and hens fed diets containing 200 and 400 mg/kg UA exhibited lower VLDL-C concentrations in the liver ( P < 0.05). The UA concentration was significantly negatively correlated with the TC levels and significantly positively correlated with the HDL-C levels in the serum ( P < 0.05; Fig. 2 C), and it was negatively correlated with the TG content and positively correlated with the TC and HDL-C contents in the liver ( P < 0.05; Fig. 2 D).

Effect of dietary urolithin A (UA) supplementation on the lipid metabolism of Roman Pink laying hens. (A) Lipid metabolism indicators in the serum (n = 10). (B) Lipid metabolism indicators in the liver (n = 6). (C) Correlation between lipid metabolism indicators in the serum and dietary UA addition. (D) Correlation between lipid metabolism indicators in the liver and dietary UA addition. Results are presented as the mean ± SEM. * P < 0.05, ⁎⁎ P < 0.01, ⁎⁎⁎ P < 0.001, and ⁎⁎⁎ P < 0.0001.

Serum and liver antioxidant capacity indicators are presented in Fig. 3 A and B, respectively. The T-SOD and GSH-Px enzyme activities and T-AOC levels in the serum and liver of the 200 mg/kg UA group were increased relative to those of the 0 mg/kg UA group ( P < 0.05). The T-SOD activity and T-AOC levels in the serum of laying hens fed the 400 mg/kg UA diet were significantly higher than those in the hens fed the CON diet ( P < 0.05). Compared with the 0 mg/kg UA group, the 200 mg/kg UA group exhibited reduced MDA levels in both the serum and liver ( P < 0.05). UA supplementation was positively correlated with the T-AOC levels in the serum and liver, positively correlated with the GSH-Px activity in the serum, and negatively correlated with the MDA levels in the serum and liver ( P < 0.05; Fig. 3 C and D).

Effect of dietary urolithin A (UA) supplementation on the antioxidant capacity of Roman Pink laying hens. (A–D) Antioxidant indicators in the serum (n = 10). (E–H) Antioxidant indicators in the liver (n = 6). (I) Correlation between antioxidant capacity indicators in the serum and dietary UA addition. (J) Correlation between antioxidant capacity indicators in the liver and dietary UA addition. Results are presented as the mean ± SEM. * P < 0.05, ⁎⁎ P < 0.01, ⁎⁎⁎ P < 0.001, and ⁎⁎⁎ P < 0.0001.

The effects of UA on the serum and liver immune function indicators in laying hens are shown in Fig. 4 A and B, respectively. In the 800 mg/kg UA group, hens showed elevated IL-6 levels in the serum and increased TNF-α levels in the liver compared with those in the CON group ( P < 0.05). In addition, the IgA levels in the liver were significantly higher in the 200, 400, and 800 mg/kg UA groups than in the CON group ( P < 0.05). Notably, the IgY level in the livers of hens supplemented with 200 mg/kg UA was significantly higher those in the livers of hens supplemented with 0 mg/kg UA ( P < 0.05). A strong positive correlation was found between the UA levels and IL-6 in the serum ( P < 0.05; Fig. 4 C) and between IgA and TNF-α in the liver ( P < 0.05; Fig. 4 D).

Effect of dietary urolithin A (UA) supplementation on the immune function of Roman Pink laying hens. (A) Immune function indicators in the serum (n = 10). (B) Immune function indicators in the liver (n = 6). (C) Correlation between immune function indicators in the serum and dietary UA addition. (D) Correlation between immune function indicators in the liver and dietary UA addition. Results are presented as the mean ± SEM. * P < 0.05, ⁎⁎ P < 0.01, ⁎⁎⁎ P < 0.001, and ⁎⁎⁎ P < 0.0001.

In addition to measuring ALT and AST activities in serum, their levels in liver tissue were assessed to evaluate hepatocyte metabolic capacity and function. These enzymes, located in the cytoplasm and mitochondria, provide insights into liver health and viability beyond serum leakage markers. The liver histopathology ( Fig. 5 A) and ALT and AST activity in the serum ( Fig. 5 B) and liver ( Fig. 5 C) of laying hens supplemented with different concentrations of UA are presented in Fig. 5 . The liver histopathological and morphological observations revealed that compared with the 0 mg/kg UA group, the 50, 200, 400, and 800 mg/kg UA groups showed no significant alteration in the hepatocyte histology and arrangement. This suggests that high doses of UA exerted minimal adverse effects on the livers of laying hens during the 6-week experimental period. The 200 mg/kg UA group showed reduced serum ALT levels compared to the 0 mg/kg UA group ( P < 0.05).

Effect of dietary urolithin A supplementation on the liver function in Roman Pink laying hens. (A) Liver histopathology (HE, × 400; n = 4). (B, C) Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) activity in the serum (n = 10). (D, E) ALT and AST activity in the liver (n = 6). Results are presented as the mean ± SEM. ⁎⁎ P < 0.01.

We chose the CON and 200 mg/kg UA groups for additional molecular experiments based on the findings related to egg production, antioxidant capacity, immune function, and lipid metabolism. The results are shown in Fig. 6 . The results showed that 200 mg/kg UA significantly elevated the mRNA levels of Nrf2, NQO1, HO-1, and GPX4 in the liver ( P < 0.05), with a strong positive correlation observed between supplementation with UA and the expression of these mRNAs ( P < 0.05; Fig. 6 F).

Effect of dietary urolithin A (UA) supplementation on the antioxidant-related genes in the liver of Roman Pink laying hens (n = 6). (A–E) The mRNA relative expression of antioxidant-related genes in the liver. (F) Correlation between antioxidant-related genes in the liver and dietary UA addition. Results are presented as the mean ± SEM. * P < 0.05, ⁎⁎ P < 0.01, and ⁎⁎⁎ P < 0.0001.

The viability of primary hepatocytes was significantly enhanced following treatment with 1, 5, and 50 μmol/L of UA, whereas the viability was reduced following treatment with 200, 400, and 800 μmol/L of UA compared with that in the CON group ( P < 0.001, Fig. 7 A). Importantly, hepatocytes treated with 5 μmol/L UA had the highest viability among all experimental groups ( P < 0.05, Fig. 7 A and B). Moreover, supplementation with 5 μmol/L UA significantly upregulated the mRNA expression of Nrf2, NQO1, HO-1, GPX4, and SLC7A11 in the primary hepatocytes ( P < 0.05, Fig. 7 C-G). In addition, supplementation with 5 μmol/L UA was significantly positively correlated with the mRNA expression levels of Nrf2, NQO1, GPX4, and SLC7A11 in the primary hepatocytes ( P < 0.05; Fig. 7 H).

Effect of urolithin A (UA) supplementation on the antioxidant-related genes in the liver primary cells of hens (n = 6). (A) Cell proliferation activity of liver primary cells detected using CCK8 assay. (B) Microscopic images of liver primary cells after incubation with 0 and 5 μmol/L for 24 h. Scale bar = 100 μm. (C–G) Relative mRNA expression of antioxidant-related genes in liver primary cells. (H) Correlation between mRNA expression of antioxidant-related genes in primary liver cells and UA treatment. Results are presented as the mean ± SEM. * P < 0.05, ⁎⁎ P < 0.01, and ⁎⁎⁎ P < 0.0001.

Compared to the CON group, the 200 mg/kg UA group showed significantly higher Nrf2 protein levels in the liver than the CON group ( P < 0.05; Fig. 8 C). Treatment with 5 μmol/L UA significantly elevated Nrf2 protein expression in the primary hepatocytes compared to treatment with 0 μmol/L UA ( P < 0.05; Fig. 8 D).

Effect of urolithin A supplementation on Nrf2 protein expression in the liver tissue and primary cells of hens (n = 3). (A,B) Representative western blot images. The levels of (C) Nrf2 in the liver tissue and (D) Nrf2 in the liver primary cells. Results are presented as the mean ± SEM. * P < 0.05 and ⁎⁎ P < 0.01.
sections.discussion:
This study demonstrates that dietary supplementation with UA exerts dose-dependent effects on aging laying hens, with 200 mg/kg identified as the optimal dosage for enhancing production performance. These improvements were associated with the activation of the hepatic Nrf2 signaling pathway, as indicated by increased Nrf2 protein levels and the upregulation of its key downstream antioxidant genes, which coincided with enhanced antioxidant capacity, modulated immune function, and improved systemic lipid homeostasis, as evidenced by reduced serum TC and TG. Higher doses (400 and 800 mg/kg) notably shifted the metabolic focus towards fat reduction and thus may compromise performance, highlighting the essential equilibrium between health modulation and productivity.

The 200 mg/kg UA treatment positively influenced egg-laying traits, with hens in this group exhibiting higher egg-laying rates and lower feed-to-egg ratios than hens in the basal feed group. Moreover, these beneficial effects were sustained throughout the trial. Although studies on the effects of UA on laying hens are lacking, a previous study reported that ellagitannins, which are metabolized to UA, enhance hen performance ( Gul et al., 2022 ). Recently, UA has attracted the attention of numerous researchers owing to its unique chemical structure and superior pharmacological properties. This compound is a key metabolite of ellagitannins produced by the intestinal microbiota, and it exhibits strong anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities, making it a promising compound for enhancing animal performance ( González-Sarrías et al., 2013 ). There were no significant differences in average daily feed intake among the treatment groups. This key finding suggests that the observed improvements in production performance at the 200 mg/kg dose of UA are not attributable to variations in feed consumption. Although 400 and 800 mg/kg of UA did not improve egg-laying traits after 6 weeks of treatment, these treatments lowered the liver and abdominal fat indices by a considerable amount. We hypothesize that administering high doses of UA (400–800 mg/kg) may excessively stimulate fatty acid oxidation and cholesterol efflux, which could lead to depleted hepatic lipid reserves and diminished abdominal fat, potentially impairing yolk precursor synthesis and egg-laying performance ( Reddy et al., 2001 ). Conversely, 200 mg/kg UA likely regulates lipid metabolism, thus maintaining the equilibrium between oviposition and metabolic activities ( Li et al., 2024 ).

Maintaining optimal lipid homeostasis is fundamental for providing energy and substrates to support reproductive processes ( Rodrigues et al., 2023 ). Our findings demonstrated that UA supplementation at a dosage of 200 mg/kg improved lipid homeostasis, as indicated by the significant reductions in serum TC and TG levels ( Wang et al., 2021 ). This optimization of hepatic lipid processing is particularly beneficial for aging hens and potentially contributes to the observed improvements in egg production and feed conversion efficiency by supporting yolk precursor availability and mitigating age-associated metabolic decline ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Yan et al., 2025 ). The observed reduction in liver and abdominal fat at higher doses (400 and 800 mg/kg), coupled with a decrease in hepatic VLDL-C levels, suggests a shift in energy partitioning away from lipid storage and possibly yolk precursor synthesis ( Han et al., 2023 ). This shift may explain the lack of further improvement in laying performance at these doses, as VLDL is a critical carrier of yolk precursors ( Chen et al., 2025 ). While this proposed change in energy distribution might reduce fat in the abdominal and liver areas, it could harm reproductive success by limiting lipids needed for yolk and egg development. Correlation analysis confirmed a dose-dependent link between UA administration and important lipid metabolism markers. However, the molecular mechanisms affecting fatty acid metabolism remain unclear. Future studies should verify these findings by examining the expression of key lipid metabolism marker genes.

In this study, administering 200 mg/kg UA to aging laying hens markedly increased the levels of T-SOD in the serum and liver, the activity of GSH-Px, and the levels of T-AOC and lowered the levels of MDA. T-SOD, GSH-Px, and T-AOC are important for protecting cells from damage caused by free radicals. Adding 200 mg/kg of UA to aging hens appeared to improve the antioxidant defense, as shown by the higher activity of these enzymes and lower levels of MDA, a harmful by-product of oxidative reactions ( Zimmermann et al., 1987 ; Wang et al., 2023 ). This increase in antioxidant capacity appeared to improve the liver health, as shown by the lower serum ALT activity, which is a sign of better hepatocyte integrity and overall liver function ( Han et al., 2020 ; Al et al., 2022 ). Immunoglobulins are essential to the immune system; consequently, their levels serve as critical indicators of immune function ( Lebedev et al., 2024 ). IgY, the main circulating antibody in birds, is similar to IgG in mammals ( Yakhkeshi et al., 2022 ). IgA is also involved in the body's immune response to infections of the mucous membranes ( Khan et al., 2018 ). Our research indicated that administering 200 mg/kg of UA to aging hens markedly increased the liver IgY and IgA levels, implying an enhancement of both systemic and mucosal immune defenses. We hypothesized that 200 mg/kg UA enhances the hepatic microenvironment by preserving the hepatic redox balance and immune homeostasis. Thus, this supplement provides a physiological basis for high egg production while also supporting normal lipid metabolism and VLDL synthesis. While 400 mg/kg UA increased certain antioxidant markers, 800 mg/kg UA concurrently elevated pro-inflammatory factors, such as serum IL-6 and hepatic TNF-α ( Jiang et al., 2022 ). This indicates that ultrahigh doses may disturb immune equilibrium and initiate low-grade inflammation. This imbalance in immune homeostasis may explain why the high-dose treatments failed to further enhance laying performance despite improving specific metabolic indicators ( Amevor et al., 2025 ).

To elucidate the mechanism through which UA exerts antioxidant and hepatoprotective effects, we focused on the Nrf2 signaling pathway, which is recognized as the principal regulator of the cellular antioxidant response ( Hayes et al., 2025 ). In vivo experiments revealed that protein and mRNA expression of Nrf2 and mRNA expression of its important downstream targets, including NQO1, HO-1 , and GPX4 , were markedly elevated in liver tissue following 200 mg/kg UA administration. Nrf2 pathway activation is the main mechanism by which UA improves hepatic antioxidant defense, as evidenced by the strong positive correlation between supplementation with UA and the expression of these genes ( Wang et al., 2024 ). We further conducted in vitro studies using primary chicken hepatocytes to validate these findings. CCK-8 assays revealed that a concentration of 5 μmol/L UA was the most effective in promoting hepatocyte proliferation, whereas concentrations of 200 μmol/L or higher were cytotoxic. Consequently, 5 μmol/L UA was selected for subsequent in vitro experiments. Prior research in mammals showed that the oral administration of 50 mg/kg of UA produces plasma concentrations of 2–3 μmol/L in addition to determining the ideal concentration for hepatocyte viability ( Larrosa et al., 2010 ). In contrast, late-laying hens consume 110–120 g of feed daily, which translates into a UA intake of 22–24 mg ( Hwang et al., 2025 ). Hepatic UA levels were compared to the effective concentrations found in mammals. Therefore, the favorable conditions generated by a dose of 200 mg/kg UA in vivo are likely to be replicated by a dose of 5 μmol/L in vitro. Our vitro data also showed that treatment with 5 μmol/L UA similarly enhanced the activation of Nrf2 and expression of its primary downstream target genes, and it also improved cell survival. The alignment of these in vivo and in vitro studies highlights UA’s capability to activate the Nrf2 pathway in hepatocytes. These findings are consistent with those of previous studies, indicating that UA enhances antioxidant defenses via the Nrf2 pathway, thereby mitigating liver damage ( Gao et al., 2022 ; Su et al., 2024 ).
sections.conclusion: This study is the first to show that dietary supplementation with 200 mg/kg UA improves laying performance in the mid production phase of aging hen. UA may improve egg production and feed efficiency by augmenting the antioxidant capacity, optimizing lipid metabolism, and enhancing immune markers, thereby fostering a healthier hepatic environment conducive to high reproductive output. The observed benefits may be attributed to Nrf2 pathway activation, which mitigates oxidative stress and promotes liver cell health. Higher doses (400–800 mg/kg) of UA resulted in the prioritization of fat reduction over egg production, likely owing to disruptions in VLDL synthesis and increased inflammation. This study's limitations include the brief 6-week trial period and small sample size for each treatment group. Therefore, these findings require validation under larger-scale, longer-term conditions, such as those spanning the entire late-laying phase in actual commercial production settings, to comprehensively assess their stability and universality. Our findings highlight the potential of 200 mg/kg UA as a plant-derived supplement to enhance the productive lifespan of laying hens by modulating liver health.
